• IUCN Red List: Endangered (severely threatened by peat-swamp destruction and agricultural conversion).
  • Wild-caught, highly specialized and endangered.
  • Adults reach approximately 3 cm (≈ 1.2″) standard length.
These fish are wild-caught, highly specialized, and endangered. Please proceed with caution. Be sure to have the habitat ready before purchase.
The Opal Licorice Gourami is endemic to Central Kalimantan in Indonesian Borneo. It has a highly restricted natural distribution.

This species inhabits extremely soft, acidic peat-swamp streams with almost no measurable mineral content. These waters are darkly stained by decomposing leaves and peat, with dense forest canopy allowing very little light to reach the surface. Its remaining peat-swamp habitat is being lost to drainage, fire, and agricultural development.

Extremely soft, acidic water is essential for wild-caught specimens.

  • pH 3.5–6.0
  • GH 0–3 °d
  • KH 0–1 °d
  • TDS preferably below 70 ppm
  • Temperature: 22–28 °C (72–82 °F); approximately 24–26 °C (75–79 °F) is suitable for routine maintenance.

For breeding, a pH of 4.0–4.5 and very low conductivity are strongly preferred. Use reverse-osmosis or similarly low-mineral water prepared with leaf litter and appropriate botanicals. Never attempt to lower the pH rapidly. Establish the correct water chemistry before introducing the fish and monitor pH carefully when KH is nearly zero. Avoid sudden temperature changes and maintain a warm, humid layer of air beneath a tightly fitted lid.
Provide driftwood, peat-safe materials, alder cones, and multiple small caves. Filtration should be gentle, preferably using an air-powered sponge filter.

A specialized micropredator that strongly prefers live food. Offer a varied diet including:

  • Live baby brine shrimp
  • Moina and small daphnia
  • Grindal worms
  • Microworms
  • Small mosquito larvae
  • Live cyclops and other tiny aquatic invertebrates

Frozen foods may eventually be accepted, but dried flakes and pellets are usually refused. A dependable supply of small live foods is essential for conditioning, maintaining body weight, and encouraging reproduction.

Secretive and delicate. Best kept as a single pair or species-only breeding group. If tankmates are necessary, choose only tiny, peaceful blackwater fishes such as:

  • Boraras
  • Sundadanio
  • Very small, gentle rasboras

Avoid larger fish, active feeders, shrimp that may disturb spawning caves, and territorial species. Never mix different Parosphromenus species. Females can be extremely difficult to identify, and closely related species may hybridize. Maintaining accurate species and collection-location information is important for conservation breeding.

When in breeding condition, males develop iridescent blue-green fin margins, intense blue bands, deep black markings, and rich red coloration in the dorsal, anal, and caudal fins. Females can be extremely difficult to identify.

A cave-spawning species with paternal care. The male selects and defends a small cave formed beneath leaf litter, wood, or another enclosed surface. Suitable artificial spawning sites include small clay caves, narrow tubes, or inverted photographic film containers.

During courtship, the male displays his iridescent fins and performs a distinctive head-down posture. The pair spawns inside the cave, where the eggs are attached to the ceiling. The male guards and tends the eggs until they hatch and continues guarding the larvae until they become free-swimming.

Newly free-swimming fry require microscopic foods such as:

  • Paramecium
  • Infusoria
  • Rotifers
  • Vinegar eels
  • Microworms
  • Newly hatched baby brine shrimp as they grow

Very soft water, abundant humic substances, and a low bacterial load are particularly important for successful egg development.

As wild-caught fish, they require extremely slow acclimation. Match the aquarium closely to their shipping water and make any necessary changes gradually. New arrivals may be pale, reclusive, or unwilling to eat. Provide dense cover, dim lighting, multiple caves, and live food immediately. Closely monitor for weight loss, rapid breathing, clamped fins, or disease following importation.

This species is listed as Endangered and has a highly restricted natural distribution.
